impl.summary: duoclip-gamesdb is implemented per SPEC.md. It has the games.json database (30 games, embedded with include_str!), strict validation with a typed DbError, from_json with a 1 MiB cap, merged, lookup, and choose_backend. choose_backend returns a Portuguese reason_pt and never puts the hook in fallbacks. The code is pure Rust with forbid(unsafe_code) and nothing in it panics on untrusted input. I added an "Implementation notes" section to SPEC.md documenting the choices the SPEC left open.
impl.checks: cargo fmt -p duoclip-gamesdb --check: clean. cargo clippy -p duoclip-gamesdb --all-targets -- -D warnings: clean. cargo test -p duoclip-gamesdb: 50 unit tests + 1 doctest pass in about 0.15 s. cargo clippy -p duoclip-gamesdb --all-targets --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu -- -D warnings: clean.
deviations_from_spec: AntiCheat::BattlEye is written "battleye" in JSON (serde rename plus alias "battl_eye"), because plain rename_all=snake_case gives the awkward "battl_eye". The docs call it battleye.
AntiCheat::Other carries #[serde(other)], so an unknown anti-cheat name from a newer remote DB is read as Other (which still blocks the hook) instead of failing the whole parse.

Extra validation beyond the SPEC: name must be non-empty; exe_names must be non-empty; exe names must be bare file names (no path separators or Windows-forbidden characters, no surrounding whitespace, non-empty stem before .exe); kernel_anticheat requires a real anti-cheat, so [None] does not count.

Hook is a primary only when it was requested (user preference Hook, or no usable preference and the game's default_backend is Hook) and every rule-3 condition holds. hook_enabled_games alone does not select it, because rule 3 lists necessary conditions.

merged: the side with the higher version wins per id and base wins on a tie. A losing-side entry whose id or exe collides with an entry already kept is dropped, so two valid DBs always merge into a valid one. Result version is the max; the winner's games come first.

Extra public items: MAX_DB_BYTES, DbError, GameEntry::has_anticheat and allows_hook, OsInfo::is_windows_11, and Default on UserPrefs. notes_pt and verified may be omitted in JSON (default empty / false), and unknown JSON fields are ignored.
embedded() returns an empty DB (version 0) instead of panicking if the embedded JSON were ever invalid. A test checks that it is not.
fallbacks are limited to the game's allowed_backends, in OS-default order. An inconsistent entry with no usable backend gets the plain OS default.
known_limitations: All anti-cheat data in games.json is best knowledge, verified=false everywhere, and several entries are marked "(a confirmar)": Marvel Rivals (modelled as Other, no kernel), League of Legends (Vanguard rollout per region), Phasmophobia (no anti-cheat). Exe names for EA FC (FC24/25/26), GTA V Enhanced and the FiveM build-specific executables should also be double-checked.

lookup matches exact basenames (Unicode-lowercased), with no wildcards. FiveM's game process name changes with the build (FiveM_bNNNN_GTAProcess.exe), so I listed known builds and newer ones will not be recognized until the DB is updated.
javaw.exe (Minecraft Java) is shared with other Java apps. As the SPEC says, matching it to Minecraft needs window-title hints later; this crate only flags it in notes_pt.
Minecraft Bedrock has no anti-cheat but does not list hook (protected Store/GDK process), which is allowed but conservative.
No game sets default_backend in the embedded data (all null), so the OS default applies until the research pass says otherwise.
